---
title: "Session 2 — Construction of the finite element method"
subtitle: "Triangular meshes, local shape functions, assembly, and numerical integration"
---

## Learning objectives

By the end of this session, students should be able to:

- define a \(P_1\) finite-element approximation space on a triangular mesh;
- construct linear nodal shape functions directly on a physical triangle;
- derive the elemental stiffness matrix and elemental load vector;
- explain how local element contributions are assembled into a global linear system;
- relate local support to matrix sparsity;
- impose homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions at nodal degrees of freedom;
- understand the practical role of the reference element and numerical quadrature.

## Schedule

| Time | Topic |
|---:|---|
| 0–15 min | Triangular mesh and definition of \(V_h\) |
| 15–35 min | \(P_1\) shape functions on one physical triangle |
| 35–50 min | Elemental stiffness matrix and load vector |
| 50–60 min | Global basis functions and assembly |
| 60–70 min | Local support, sparsity, and Dirichlet conditions |
| 70–90 min | Technical block: reference element, mapping, and quadrature |

---

# Triangular mesh and finite-element space

Let

$$
\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2
$$

be approximated by a triangulation

$$
\mathcal{T}_h
=
\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_{N_e}\}.
$$

The domain is decomposed into non-overlapping triangles:

$$
\Omega_h
=
\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h} T.
$$

For linear triangular finite elements, we define

$$
\boxed{
V_h
=
\left\{
v_h\in C^0(\Omega_h)
:
v_h|_T\in\mathbb{P}_1(T)
\quad
\forall T\in\mathcal{T}_h
\right\}.
}
$$

Thus a finite-element function is:

- continuous over the whole mesh;
- affine on each individual triangle.

For homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions,

$$
u=0
\qquad\text{on }\partial\Omega,
$$

the approximation space is restricted to functions satisfying

$$
v_h=0
\qquad\text{on }\partial\Omega.
$$

The finite-element approximation is written

$$
u_h(x,y)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N_h}
U_i\phi_i(x,y),
$$

where the global nodal functions satisfy

$$
\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_j)
=
\delta_{ij}.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{
U_i=u_h(\mathbf{x}_i).
}
$$

The coefficients of the finite-element approximation are directly the nodal values of the approximate solution.

---

# \(P_1\) shape functions on one physical triangle

Consider one triangle

$$
T
=
\operatorname{conv}
\{
\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\mathbf{x}_3
\},
$$

with

$$
\mathbf{x}_i=(x_i,y_i).
$$

Inside \(T\), the finite-element solution is affine:

$$
u_h|_T(x,y)
=
U_1N_1(x,y)
+
U_2N_2(x,y)
+
U_3N_3(x,y).
$$

The local shape functions are affine functions

$$
N_i(x,y)
=
a_i+b_i x+c_i y,
$$

defined by the nodal interpolation conditions

$$
\boxed{
N_i(\mathbf{x}_j)=\delta_{ij}.
}
$$

Thus

$$
N_1(\mathbf{x}_1)=1,
\qquad
N_1(\mathbf{x}_2)=N_1(\mathbf{x}_3)=0,
$$

and similarly for \(N_2\) and \(N_3\).

The local approximation therefore satisfies

$$
u_h(\mathbf{x}_i)=U_i.
$$

---

## Explicit construction

For each shape function,

$$
N_i(x,y)=a_i+b_i x+c_i y,
$$

the three coefficients are obtained by solving a \(3\times3\) system.

For example, for \(N_1\),

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_1 & y_1\\
1 & x_2 & y_2\\
1 & x_3 & y_3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
a_1\\
b_1\\
c_1
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
0\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Likewise,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_1 & y_1\\
1 & x_2 & y_2\\
1 & x_3 & y_3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
a_2\\
b_2\\
c_2
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
1\\
0
\end{pmatrix},
$$

and

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_1 & y_1\\
1 & x_2 & y_2\\
1 & x_3 & y_3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
a_3\\
b_3\\
c_3
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Because the functions are affine,

$$
\boxed{
\nabla N_i
=
\begin{pmatrix}
b_i\\
c_i
\end{pmatrix}
}
$$

is constant over the triangle.

This property makes the \(P_1\) Poisson element particularly simple.

---

# Elemental stiffness matrix

For the Poisson problem,

$$
-\Delta u=f,
$$

the weak form involves

$$
a(u,v)
=
\int_\Omega
\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,d\Omega.
$$

On one triangle \(T\), the elemental stiffness matrix is defined by

$$
\boxed{
K^{(T)}_{ij}
=
\int_T
\nabla N_i\cdot\nabla N_j\,d\Omega.
}
$$

Since the gradients of the \(P_1\) shape functions are constant on \(T\),

$$
\nabla N_i\cdot\nabla N_j
$$

is also constant.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
K^{(T)}_{ij}
=
|T|
\,
\nabla N_i\cdot\nabla N_j.
}
$$

The full elemental matrix is

$$
K^{(T)}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
K^{(T)}_{11} & K^{(T)}_{12} & K^{(T)}_{13}\\
K^{(T)}_{21} & K^{(T)}_{22} & K^{(T)}_{23}\\
K^{(T)}_{31} & K^{(T)}_{32} & K^{(T)}_{33}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

---

# Elemental load vector

The right-hand side of the weak formulation is

$$
\ell(v)
=
\int_\Omega fv\,d\Omega.
$$

On one triangle,

$$
\boxed{
F_i^{(T)}
=
\int_T
fN_i\,d\Omega.
}
$$

Thus

$$
F^{(T)}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
F_1^{(T)}\\
F_2^{(T)}\\
F_3^{(T)}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For constant \(f\), one may use

$$
\int_T N_i\,d\Omega
=
\frac{|T|}{3},
$$

so that

$$
\boxed{
F^{(T)}
=
\frac{f|T|}{3}
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
1\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$

For a more general \(f(x,y)\), the integral generally needs to be evaluated numerically.

> **FEM localizes both approximation and integration.**

---

# From local to global basis functions

A global nodal basis function \(\phi_i\) is constructed by joining the local shape functions associated with node \(i\) over all triangles that contain that node.

Thus,

$$
\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_j)=\delta_{ij},
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{supp}\phi_i
=
\bigcup
\left\{
T\in\mathcal{T}_h:
\mathbf{x}_i\in T
\right\}.
$$

The support of \(\phi_i\) is therefore local.

The global approximation is

$$
u_h
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N_h}
U_i\phi_i.
$$


```{python}
#| label: fig-gmsh-mesh
#| fig-cap: "Triangular mesh of a square domain containing a circular hole."
#| echo: true

import gmsh
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.tri as mtri

gmsh.initialize()
gmsh.model.add("square_with_hole")

# Geometry
L = 1.0
R = 0.18

# Square
square = gmsh.model.occ.addRectangle(0, 0, 0, L, L)

# Circular hole
disk = gmsh.model.occ.addDisk(0.5, 0.5, 0, R, R)

# Boolean subtraction
domain, _ = gmsh.model.occ.cut(
    [(2, square)],
    [(2, disk)]
)

gmsh.model.occ.synchronize()

# Typical mesh size
gmsh.option.setNumber("Mesh.MeshSizeMin", 0.1)
gmsh.option.setNumber("Mesh.MeshSizeMax", 0.2)

# Generate 2D triangular mesh
gmsh.model.mesh.generate(2)

# ----------------------------------
# Extract nodes
# ----------------------------------

node_tags, node_coords, _ = gmsh.model.mesh.getNodes()

coords = node_coords.reshape(-1, 3)

x = coords[:, 0]
y = coords[:, 1]

# Gmsh node tags are not necessarily 0,1,2,...
tag_to_index = {
    tag: i for i, tag in enumerate(node_tags)
}

# ----------------------------------
# Extract triangular elements
# ----------------------------------

element_types, element_tags, element_nodes = \
    gmsh.model.mesh.getElements(dim=2)

triangles = None

for element_type, nodes in zip(element_types, element_nodes):

    # 3-node linear triangle
    if element_type == 2:

        nodes = nodes.reshape(-1, 3)

        triangles = np.array([
            [tag_to_index[tag] for tag in tri]
            for tri in nodes
        ])

        break

gmsh.finalize()

# ----------------------------------
# Plot using Matplotlib
# ----------------------------------

mesh = mtri.Triangulation(x, y, triangles)

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6))

plt.triplot(mesh, linewidth=0.7)
plt.plot(x, y, ".", markersize=2)

plt.xlabel("$x$")
plt.ylabel("$y$")
plt.gca().set_aspect("equal")

plt.show()
```


```{python}
# -------------------------------------------------
# Choose one interior node
# -------------------------------------------------

# Select the node closest to this point
target_point = np.array([0.25, 0.50])

i = np.argmin(
    (x - target_point[0])**2
    +
    (y - target_point[1])**2
)

# Global nodal basis function:
# phi_i = 1 at node i and 0 at every other node

phi = np.zeros(len(x))
phi[i] = 1.0

# -------------------------------------------------
# Plot mesh and basis function
# -------------------------------------------------

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9, 6))

ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")

ax.plot_trisurf(
    mesh,
    phi,
    edgecolor="black",
    linewidth=0.7,
    alpha=0.9
)

# Highlight selected node
ax.scatter(
    [x[i]],
    [y[i]],
    [1],
    s=60
)

ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
ax.set_zlabel(r"$\phi_i$")

ax.set_title("Global nodal basis function")

plt.show()
```



---

# Assembly of the global system

Suppose the local nodes

$$
1,\qquad 2,\qquad 3
$$

of one triangle correspond to the global nodes

$$
5,\qquad 12,\qquad 8.
$$

Then the elemental stiffness matrix is assembled by adding its entries to the corresponding entries of the global matrix:

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
K_{5,5} & K_{5,12} & K_{5,8}\\
K_{12,5} & K_{12,12} & K_{12,8}\\
K_{8,5} & K_{8,12} & K_{8,8}
\end{pmatrix}
\; += \;
\begin{pmatrix}
K^{(T)}_{11} & K^{(T)}_{12} & K^{(T)}_{13}\\
K^{(T)}_{21} & K^{(T)}_{22} & K^{(T)}_{23}\\
K^{(T)}_{31} & K^{(T)}_{32} & K^{(T)}_{33}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
F_5\\
F_{12}\\
F_8
\end{pmatrix}
\; += \;
\begin{pmatrix}
F^{(T)}_1\\
F^{(T)}_2\\
F^{(T)}_3
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

After assembling all triangles,

$$
\boxed{KU=F.}
$$

---

# Local support and sparsity

The global stiffness entries are

$$
K_{ij}
=
\int_\Omega
\nabla\phi_i\cdot\nabla\phi_j\,d\Omega.
$$

If two nodal basis functions do not overlap,

$$
\operatorname{supp}\phi_i
\cap
\operatorname{supp}\phi_j
=
\varnothing,
$$

then

$$
K_{ij}=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\text{local support}
\Longrightarrow
\text{sparse global matrix}.
}
$$

Only nodes that belong to at least one common element can interact directly in the stiffness matrix.

---

# Dirichlet boundary conditions

For homogeneous Dirichlet conditions,

$$
u=0
\qquad
\text{on }\partial\Omega,
$$

the finite-element coefficients associated with boundary nodes are prescribed:

$$
\boxed{
U_i=0
\qquad
\text{for all boundary nodes }i.
}
$$

The remaining unknowns correspond to interior nodes.

Non-homogeneous Dirichlet conditions

Suppose some nodal values are prescribed by the Dirichlet condition

$$
u=g
\qquad \text{on } \Gamma_D.
$$

We split the degrees of freedom into

- \(U_f\): unknown (free) degrees of freedom,
- \(U_D\): prescribed Dirichlet degrees of freedom.

After grouping the corresponding rows and columns, the global system

$$
KU=F
$$

can be written as

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
K_{ff} & K_{fD}\\
K_{Df} & K_{DD}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
U_f\\
U_D
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
F_f\\
F_D
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The Dirichlet values are known:

$$
U_D=g_D.
$$

We therefore substitute them into the equations corresponding to the
unknown degrees of freedom:

$$
K_{ff}U_f + K_{fD}g_D = F_f,
$$

or

$$
\boxed{
K_{ff}U_f
=
F_f-K_{fD}g_D.
}
$$

The unknown nodal values \(U_f\) are obtained by solving this reduced system.
The complete solution is then reconstructed from

$$
U=
\begin{pmatrix}
U_f\\
g_D
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

---

# Technical block — Why a reference element?

The previous derivation was carried out directly on a physical triangle.

This is sufficient to understand the finite-element method.

In practical finite-element software, however, one wants a systematic way to evaluate integrals on many differently shaped elements.

Instead of developing a different integration procedure on every triangle, one introduces a single standard triangle.

---

## Reference triangle

Define the reference triangle

$$
\widehat T
=
\left\{
(\xi,\eta):
\xi\ge0,\quad
\eta\ge0,\quad
\xi+\eta\le1
\right\}.
$$

Its vertices are

$$
(0,0),
\qquad
(1,0),
\qquad
(0,1).
$$

Every physical triangle \(T\) can be obtained from \(\widehat T\) through an affine transformation.

---

## Affine mapping

Let the reference triangle be

$$
\hat T
=
\left\{
(\xi,\eta):
\xi\ge 0,\;
\eta\ge 0,\;
\xi+\eta\le 1
\right\}.
$$

A physical triangle \(T\), with vertices
\(\mathbf x_1,\mathbf x_2,\mathbf x_3\), is obtained through the affine mapping

$$
\mathbf x(\xi,\eta)
=
\mathbf x_1
+
\xi(\mathbf x_2-\mathbf x_1)
+
\eta(\mathbf x_3-\mathbf x_1).
$$

Its Jacobian is

$$
J
=
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(\xi,\eta)}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
x_2-x_1 & x_3-x_1\\
y_2-y_1 & y_3-y_1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The area element transforms as

$$
\boxed{
d\Omega
=
|\det J|\,d\xi\,d\eta.
}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_T g(x,y)\,d\Omega
=
\int_{\hat T}
g(\mathbf x(\xi,\eta))
|\det J|
\,d\xi\,d\eta.
$$

For the Poisson bilinear form,

$$
K^{(T)}_{ij}
=
\int_T
\nabla N_i\cdot\nabla N_j
\,d\Omega,
$$

the change of variables gives

$$
K^{(T)}_{ij}
=
\int_{\hat T}
\left(J^{-T}\nabla_{\xi}\hat N_i\right)
\cdot
\left(J^{-T}\nabla_{\xi}\hat N_j\right)
|\det J|
\,d\xi\,d\eta.
$$

Using quadrature on the reference element,

$$
\boxed{
K^{(T)}_{ij}
\approx
\sum_{q=1}^{n_q}
w_q\,
\left(
J^{-T}\nabla_{\xi}\hat N_i
\right)_{\!q}
\cdot
\left(
J^{-T}\nabla_{\xi}\hat N_j
\right)_{\!q}
\,|\det J_q|.
}
$$

More generally, the elemental load vector is computed as

$$
\boxed{
F^{(T)}_i
\approx
\sum_{q=1}^{n_q}
w_q\,
f(\mathbf x_q)\,
\hat N_i(\xi_q,\eta_q)\,
|\det J_q|.
}
$$

For an affine \(P_1\) triangle, \(J\) is constant over the element, so

$$
J_q = J
$$

for every quadrature point.

### Transformation of gradients

If a shape function on the physical element is obtained from a reference
shape function,

$$
N_i(x,y)
=
\hat N_i(\xi,\eta),
$$

then the chain rule gives

$$
\nabla_{\xi}\hat N_i
=
J^T \nabla_x N_i.
$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
\nabla_x N_i
=
J^{-T}\nabla_{\xi}\hat N_i.
}
$$

The elemental stiffness matrix can therefore be computed entirely on the
reference triangle:

$$
\boxed{
K^{(T)}_{ij}
=
\int_{\hat T}
\left(J^{-T}\nabla_{\xi}\hat N_i\right)
\cdot
\left(J^{-T}\nabla_{\xi}\hat N_j\right)
|\det J|
\,d\xi\,d\eta.
}
$$

For an affine \(P_1\) triangle, \(J\) and the reference gradients are constant,
so the integrand is constant over the element.

---

## Transforming an integral

An integral over a physical triangle,

$$
\int_T g(x,y)\,d\Omega,
$$

can therefore be written as

$$
\boxed{
\int_{\widehat T}
g(x(\xi,\eta),y(\xi,\eta))
|\det J|
\,d\xi\,d\eta.
}
$$

The important practical idea is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{all element integrations can be reduced to integration over the same reference triangle.}
}
$$

---

# 10. Numerical quadrature

In general, finite-element integrals are evaluated numerically.

On the reference triangle,

$$
\int_{\widehat T}
g(\xi,\eta)\,d\xi\,d\eta
$$

is approximated by

$$
\boxed{
\sum_{q=1}^{N_q}
w_q\,g(\xi_q,\eta_q).
}
$$

Hence, on a physical triangle,

$$
\boxed{
\int_T
g(x,y)\,d\Omega
\approx
\sum_{q=1}^{N_q}
w_q\,
g(x(\xi_q,\eta_q),y(\xi_q,\eta_q))
|\det J|.
}
$$

For the simplest one-point quadrature rule on the reference triangle, the integration point is the centroid

$$
(\xi_q,\eta_q)
=
\left(
\frac13,\frac13
\right).
$$

Since

$$
|\widehat T|=\frac12,
$$

the corresponding weight is

$$
w_q=\frac12.
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{
\int_{\widehat T}g(\xi,\eta)\,d\xi\,d\eta
\approx
\frac12
g\left(\frac13,\frac13\right).
}
$$

This rule is exact for affine functions.

---

# 11. Practical finite-element algorithm

For the Poisson problem, a basic finite-element code follows the sequence:

1. Generate a triangular mesh.
2. Define the nodal degrees of freedom.
3. For each triangle \(T\):
   - construct the local shape functions;
   - compute \(K^{(T)}\);
   - compute \(F^{(T)}\);
   - add these contributions to the global \(K\) and \(F\).
4. Impose Dirichlet boundary conditions.
5. Solve

   $$
   KU=F.
   $$

6. Reconstruct

   $$
   u_h(x,y)
   =
   \sum_i U_i\phi_i(x,y).
   $$

The central computational structure is therefore

$$
\boxed{
\text{mesh}
\rightarrow
\text{local approximation}
\rightarrow
\text{element integrals}
\rightarrow
\text{assembly}
\rightarrow
\text{sparse global system}.
}
$$
